I know of nothing better than a piece of thick bar-iron, flattened at the end to an al- most sharp edge, and bent over about two inches of its length at right angle, for clean- ing the carbon deposit from cylinder head and piston top. But an old blunt table knife is most convenient for removing the deposit from around the valve pockets, exhaust- union and pocket BENEATH the valve. Special attention should be paid• to the‘ valve pocket, obviously, any deposit of carbon here will re- strict the entrance of fresh gas and the exit of exhaust gases. Another point which should be specially attended to is the rim which is in- variably found in the cylinder just above the top of the stroke of the piston. Try to get every particle of carbon away, leaving at least no lumps. It is these lumps which, becoming incandescent, cause pre-ignition and knocking on hills. In the old days of accumulator igni- tion I have seen a dirty engine fire away merrily and regularly for five minutes or so after the current had been switched off, this being entirely due to incandescent carbon. Personally, I finish off the piston head and cylinder top with coarse emery paper.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 8, 1916 GUARDIANS' CHOICE.
Licensed Victualler Preferred To A Clergyman.
CULTURE AND BUSINESS.

Offered the Choice of a clergyman- and a licensed victualler, who were nominated for a vacancy on the Board, the Guardians, at their meeting on Wednesday., decided in favour ox the licensed victualler.

The relative merits and abilities of the two ,candidates for the position were placed before the Board by their supporters for a considerable time, prominent among them being the Rev.' A. M. Mitchell and Mr. W. J. Shaw.

The district requiring representation was the Crow-lane Ward of the Parish of Newton-in- Makerfield, and the two candidates nominated were the Rev. Bertram Eustace Taylor, of Cross- lane, Earlestown, and Mr. Thomas Siddeley, licensed victualler, 1, Railway-street, Earles- town. A third candidate, Mr. J. A. Rushworth, also a licensed victualler, of 212. Winwick-road. Warrington, had been nominated, but had with- drawn.

The claims of Mr. Siddeley were first put for- ward by Mr. W. C. Brooks, who proposed .that he should-be elected. In doing SO he paid tribute to Mr. Siddeley's qualities, and the interest he took in public affairs. Mr. • Bent supported, and speaking of the can- didate's abilities, thought they could not make a better choice than select Mr. Siddeley.

div.head: AN EXCELLENT PARSON.
div.p: AN EXCELLENT PARSON.

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, pressed the claims Of his colleague in holy orders. Before ho referred to Mr. Taylor's abilities, he poked fun at the licensed victuallers by. declaring that he was somewhat 'surprised that Mr. Brooks had not withdrawn the name of Mr. Siddeley as showing his thankfulness for having-Such a „delightful Budget for the Trade—no 'extra taxation on beer or spirits. Mr,,Shaw• intervened with a remark that the ; teetotallers were now being taxed---coffee and Icocoa drinkers.

Proceeding, the Rev. A. M. Mitchell said his ministerial colleague was an excellent man. "I don't say that because he is a parson," continued the speaker. "All _parsons are not excellent." (Hear, hear, and laughter.)- Mr. Taylor was an indefatigable worker, and would be a most valu- able addition to the Board. He was the only clergyman from his (Mr. Mitchell's) district who troubled to come to the 'Workhouse to visit the sic* with anything like regularity. He was good and kindly, and, as a , man of culture, he would tend to raise the tone of the Board. They had -already reached celestial heights, but they Could sear to still higher heights. • Mr. W. J. Show wanted to know more about the Rev. Mr. Mitchell's "dearly beloved alum in cloth." He was not " reverenerng " him ! He understood that Mr. Taylor had only been in the neighbourhood 15 or 18 Months.

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell': Nonsense! He has been threc,or four years. . . Mr. Shaw said in Mr. Siddeley they had a man Who. had lived the whole • of his life in the dis-: trict and was an upright and honourable man He was not of 'military age like Mr. Taylor, and if that 'gentleman was such a good- Young man as they were led to believe, his goodness and his. abilities would be very valuable at. the Front.
Mr. Seton said Mr. 'Taylor had been in Earlos- town about seven years, and was about 40 years of age. _

Tho, Chairman (Mr. A. J. Jolley) intimated that he had a letter bearing on the subject. Mr. Brooks thouelit the letter should not be read, and the Chairman announced that as there was likely to be objection he would not read it.
Miss Broadbent sunported the nomination Of Mr. Taylor, remarking that . she felt sure he would take a great interest in the work.
ANOTHER HORATIO! •

div.p: PoULTRY FOR PRoFiT.
THE YOUNG BIRDS.

The young stock claim by far the greater Part of one's attention at the present moment. There are by this time . probably several batches of chickens running about ranging from a few days to a couple of months old. These birds represent considerable value, as they will be ready for marketing in the coursel of the next month or two, and will therefore participate in the extremely high prices. that are procurable during the spring. months. Im- mediately they are large enough, they should. be fattened and packed off to market, or else, disposed of to the higglers for reselling to the large fattening establishments. The farmer who possesses well-developed and white-fleshed chic•kens 'during the spring can ,almost ask his oWn.. price, as the rivalry is so exceptionally keen among .the fatteners, A point that should never be forgotten in this connection is that it pa.l s much better to market elockens during the spring weighing, say, t!lb. to 211 b.. each, than to keep them until they weigh half as much 'again, for by the time.they have attained to this size prices will, in all -probability, have fallen, andeno more money will be secured ,for them, against which must be reckoned the cost of their food, the labour involved in attending to them, and the space occupied. The very young chickens require careful treatment dur- ing the present month, for the Weather is often so changeable that chills are of frequent iccurrence. Whenever the 'weather permits, the chickens, even those that are only a week or' a fortnight old, should :have access to e grass run, and should have plenty ,of fresh air, as these are essential to successful rearing. So far as the older chickens are concerned— those that were brought out early in the year— they should be housed in warm and well- ventilated sheds. which are perfectly dry and free from -draughts. Those who intend to market. their own birds should go to the trouble of preparing them suitably. For two or three weeks before killing : the chickens should be confined in a coop or small shed, and allowed as little exercise as Possible, in order to encourage the production of flesh. They .should be fed three times a day on mash and not grain, as the former is so much more easily assimilated. Ground oats moistened with skim milk is the best food, providing flesh of first-class texture and colour. . .

Feather eating seems to be More prevalent this. season - than ever,- probably due to the fact that the bad. weather We have had has necessitated keeping:the birds indoors so much. Some authorities on parasitic life have put feather-picking down to a parasite, aml many different remedies have been suggested. I have Very 'minutely examined ..fowls affected in this way—both those that pick their 'own feathers and also those that OM: the feathers of other birds. I think 'that lam quite justified in saying that for every bird that picks its own feathers' there must be a hundred that pick feathers from .other. birds, This, to .my way of thinking, seems to do away with: the parasite tlieory. No doubt in Seine cases it is caused by a parasite, but there are hundreds of such birds, upon which no, trace of insects can be found. -. Very little appears tn.be known about this vicious habit—probably this is a' more correct term than disease. It is very often. claimed as the reason for this habit' that the birds are not getting animal food; the. cause ig also suggested that they are getting too much animal :food, thus :causing the body to become too heated; lack of grit, and no green food, are also given . the :raison- d'etre for this disgusting . habit, which .absoltitely spoils the appearance of the *hole pen. The birds to be placed in the breeding pen should be in perfect -health--i.e., they should not only be free from disease, but. they should show vigour and activity. Sometimes there are existing agencies which can give the necessary help—perhaps a firm or its benevolent fund, or a parochial fund, or an endowel chit raj. In other cases, at the instance of the Guild, bad debts have been cancelled, costly, conval- escent treatment secured, additional pensions procured, life insurance claims recovered, or weekly money grants made. . ,But, of course, there remain many cases where material help must somehow be procured. The system adopted is called the "Stand-by" sys- tem. It .means that someone is asked to stand by a less fortunate fellow-townsman in his dis- tress and meet his needs for a short time. A request may be 'made for milk, for convales- cent treatment, for a• hawker's licence, for a weekly allowance during illness, ,for the supply of boots, clogs, Warm clothing, coal, or nourish- ment. Money and goods given for such purposes are always under the control of a District Committee and are used entirely for the bene- fit of ,the Persons assisted. Not a penny is ukedl for office, expenses, and consequently such money does not appear in the Guild accounts. It is therefore open to the public to give financial help inwo <different ways. The " Stand-by " helps a particular family or indi- vidual in difficulties. ,The annual subscriber to the: guild Funds maintains the organisation through • which such' material help is given, 'and sustains the, educational and constructive work to Which reference .has . been made. Some people help in one way, some in another, while some again 'help in both ways. Others do neither, and this may be,. not because they< are unwilling to .help to bear the burdens .of, others, but because they have not hitherto understood the principles and . the activities of the Guild,of Help. div.head: FINANCIAL STRENGTH OF ENGLAND.
div.p: THE FINANCIAL STRENGTH OF ENGLAND.
Tile
[uestion of how and when the u=ar will

end depends in a large measure upon the relative financial resources of Germany and Great Britain. Victory by arms stands first, but this largely depends upon money, for no country can fight without resources, and thcise in all the belligerent countries are diminish- ing. The Budget speech of the Chancellor of the Exchequer has put clearly before the country the monetary strength of England,

and her ability to continue the war and wear down Germany. First as to income. The new taxes and the addition g to existing taxes proposed by Mr. McKenna will yield £151,000,000. Included in this is the whole yield of the excess profit tax. lie taxes and other sources of revenue in operation before the war brought in £163,000,000; which with taxes levied since the war in previous Budgets and in this Budget grows into an income of over £500,000,000 for the current
year. Germany has, so far, raised nothing by taxes for war expenditure. She is now hesitating about measures which may yield £24,000,000.

We began the war with a national debt of £600,000,000. At the end of the present financial year, March, 1917, calculating ate same war expenditure, we shall have a national debt of £3,443,000,000. Against this we shall have lent to our Allies £800,000,000, leaving a net increase of £2,643,000,000, which represents our in- creased national liability. This involves an annual debt charge in interest and sinking fund (required to extinguish the debt in thirty-seven years) of £145,000,000. After deducting the interest on our old debt we shall have to bear an additional annual burden of about £115,000,000. Since our revenue in pre-war• time was £163,000,000, our additional taxes for thirty-seven years will be two-. thirds extra. This would mean that of the £506,000,000, which this year we shall apparently have to pay, about £200,000,000 can be taken off in *relief of present taxat;on. But against this it should be temembei ed that we &innot depend n tha excess profit tax as a permanent source of income.

Turning to our present expenditure, after deducting loans to our Allies, we are spend- ing a little over three millions a day on the I war, of which we are raising about one million by revenue, leaving two millions to be raised by loans. This, of course, leaves out the amount we have to raise to lend to our Allies which, for the time being, we assume to be recoverable, with interest, although it is doubtful if we Shall ever recover it as a whole. This, of course, is on the presumption that our expenditure remains the same, a state of things for which we can hardly hope. We may, however, reasonably anticipate that should the war terminate before the next annual Budget appears the Chancellor will be able to take off a considerable proportion of the present taxes.

In regard to the taxes to be levied under the present Budget, no serious objection can be raised agatst them in detail. It is practically impossible, to levy any tax that does not press unfailly in individual cases. The income tax is wisely graduated. It, of course, bears heavily on large incomes, but the very fact of having a large income indi- cates greater ability to pay. The greakst strain will be experienced by those with fixed incomes,. who have larger expenses .to meet through dearer products, and heavier income tax as well,, and an adjustment to fixed in- comes wherever it is possible, is much to be desired.

11/4Totwithstarxding Robert Lowe's experience of burning his fingers over the match tax, the match tax, in the present circumstances, is a good one. Matches being so cheap, are used wastefully, and smokers must revert to the old-fashioned spills.' Further, the wood, it is vnderstood, come; from kEr oad, and this takes up a good deal of tonnage, which can ill be spared. -

The tax on travelling is open to question. The large bulk of it will be paid by people on business. If it could be restricted—which it cannot—to those on pleasure bent, it could be classed as a tax on amusements. The tax is only expected to bring in k 3,000,000, one day's war expenditure, and will involve a good deal of expense to collect. The motor car tax is reasonable, but exemption should be made—although it is difficult—for those ,who use Tutors for business and professional prirposes.

It is satisfactory that no further import duties have been imposed. Taxes on a mis- cellaneous number of articles are very ex- pensive to collect. We have neither the staff - nor the accommodation at our many ports to gather these and to inspect the goods. The expensive freights are of themselves a serious handicap to the importation of goods, and give the- home manufacturers a great advantage. .If they Cannot with this help command -the market there is something latogr with -their .taanufactot.,.

div.head: CHEER° !
div.p: CHEER° !

There were not enough Germans ever born to de, press the men at the Front.... When they get good billets. they say to each other, "Cheero!"; when they get poor billets, or only a little straw in a-leaky hovel, they still say "Cheero!"; and all they ask is that folks at home should adopt the same attitude and say " Cheero!" toe. —Captain William Redmond, M.P., in House of Commons, 16th March, 1916.

When the -men in the trenches are weary and spent, And the roar of the grim guns dies away. And into their billets they creep content At the trying close of a dreadful day, They cast all anxious cares aside, And they light their" pipes as the sun sinks low, And cry through the gloom, to the world outside: " Cheer° !"

When they reel back wounded, and leave behind The pallid forms of their noble dead, And, nipped with the piercing winter,wind, They crawl to the straw in some leaky shed, And fling their poor tired limbs on the floor, While the sky is lit with the battle-glow, They turn to each other and call once more: " Cheero !" - • -

Out on the sodden fields of France, Or far away on the' desert sands, Wherever the devil may lead the dance, The gallant figure in khaki stands. All the Germans who ever were born, Staking all on the final blow, Will fly before him Kim° shining morn: " Cheer° •

Shall we grumble and grouse at home When every lad is a lion there, Or send to greet them across the foam An answering word that shall kill despair, And light new fires in the lands afar, And shatter the hopes of the cruel foe, And. bring- thisiielliph • ". Cheer.° !"„ Alai :Wig Altman.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 8, 1916 AFTER-THE-WAR THE PLEASURE TAX. HARI OF MRS. JAS. SMETHURST PROBLEMS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 8, 1916 AFTER-THE-WAR THE PLEASURE TAX. HARI OF MRS. JAS. SMETHURST PROBLEMS.
Sir Arthur Crosfield And The
Dangers Of Recklessness.
THE SUGGESTED PEACE
TERMS.
To the Editor of "The Examiner.'!

Sir,—l shall not this week venture to trespass on your space at any very: great length, nor, while making a few references to post-war problems, have I any inclinatibn to write, or intention •of writing, dogmatically.. I much fipreferlor The most Part to.cOntent myself With 'putting a few-qUestions. It nia.Y.,be said: "Why refer to post-war problems .at ill? It is im- possible toloreca.st the conditions under which negotiations for peace will be opened, and, therefore, without all the facts _before 'us, im- possible to crystalise 'thought and. impression into definite opinioii and conviction ." Certainly. I. do 'not -dispute this. But still' theie is a great deal of discussion going on up and down the country in one circle and another as to the terms on which the Allies should insist, when they are in a position to insist 'up:six them be- fore making peace, and as to. the policies that should then be .adopted; and it is in this con- nection I propose to ask a few questions. Besides great Cessions of territory to be made ,by Austria and Turkey, and perhaps some ' smaller cessions by Germany to Russia; Besides the acquisition of Alsace and Lorraine by France and very large areas of overeea terri- tory by the British Empire; and besides what is ceded by Austria to Italy, it is argued that Prance. Belgium and Serbia must receive in- demnities on a scale that will run into thou,- sands.of millions of pounds:. But there are. also psople who go the extreme length Of urging , that not only should the Central Powers and Turkey and Bulgaria be forced to concede terri- tory on an enormons•scale, but that Germany, as one of the most powerful and predominant Commercial nations of the world; should cease to exist.. • They would leave enough of the population of Germany to cultivate its soil, but to a large extent its manufacturing population would scarcely he left any alternative except that of emigration. . There are, in fact, scarcely any limits to the drastic, measures which men of this way of thinking would take. Now if such a policy were adopted the first question one naturally asks is: Where would France and Belgium and Serbia get one Penny of the enormous indemnities due to them?, And at once there arises the further question as to whether even the threat of terms of that character would not inevitably postpone the cessation of hostilities beyond the time. when otherwise it would be Open to the Allies to insist on and obtain satisfactory terms of peace.
ECONOMIC PRESSURE TO SHORTEN THE WAR.

Supposing, then, that a policy of this extreme! character should be for several reasons not considered practicable or I desirable by the ' Allies, what are the. other alternatives before, them? The first (of which we have heard a l great" deal lately) is the attempt to check Ger.; man economic and commercial development by concerted action of the Allies, including the adoption of ,protective duties by Great Britain. We are urged to impose these duties in order, on the one hand, to inflict commercial loss on Germany, and on the other for the pnepose of strengthening, by motives of self-interest and united interest, the ties which at present bind the Allied 'Powers together. It is. here that,one is -bound to ask several questions. - We are officially_ informed that the conference of the Allies to be held in Paris, probably to- wards the end of April, will consider in what way, by concerted action, they may be able to bring to bear the utmost commercial and economic pressure upon the Central Powers; of course with the object of shortening the war. It goes without saying that whatever Steps the distinguished representatives of the Allied Powers decide to be necessary for this purpose we .shill support them to a man. Then it is suggested that as at the conclusion of the war Germany will attempt to dump into our mar- kets enormous and altogether abnormal quan- tities of the manufactures she has been accumulating during the war, and for which she has been unable to find her customary markets abroad, we shall require to impose temporary Protective duties to prevent partial dislocation of our trade by this contemplated German policy. We are asked, and I think not unreasonably, to keep an open and unbiassed mind fOr the consideration of that /very big problem when it arrives. .

div.head: FULL-BLOODED PROTECTION.
div.p: FULL-BLOODED PROTECTION.

But then we are asked to do a good deal more; we are invited to adopt forthwith a full- blooded and permanent policy of Protection for this country, with an elaborate and con- comitant system of Preferential tariffs. To what extent shall we differentiate in the duties! on goods coming into our markets, and what will be the consequences? It is intended that the heaviest duties should be placed upon the goods sent us by Germany and Austria, or at any rate upon the goods that come from the Fatherland. A somewhat lower scale of duties would be imposed upon the goods sent us by the Neutral Powers. But are we, then, to give our Allies a prefer- ence over the Neutral Powers by a third scale of duties somewhat lower than the second scale? And, finally, if in the imposition of these duties we wish to give our own kith and kin in the Colonies better terms than we give to any one else, ,that will mean a fourth scale of duties. It will be the lowest scale of all, but none the less it will mean the imposition of new duties upon goods which at the present time our Colonies send entirely free of duty into our markets. Will not that strike them as a very strange way of expressing in practical fashion the admiration which is felt from end to end of Britain for the splendid patriotism and Imperial spirit that has been shown through- out our great Colonial Empire? Let us never for one moment forget that it would be impos- sible to set up this vast and complex system of preferential tariffs, while at the same time continuing to give our Colonies the benefit of the same British Free Trade conditions as they enjoy to-day. As it is important that this point should be made quite clear, I give in proof of it a suffi- ciently significant illustration of it which occurred the other day.

div.head: AGRICULTURAL STUMBLING-BLOCK.
div.p: AGRICULTURAL STUMBLING-BLOCK.

The Associated Chambers of Commerce had drafted a resolution declaring that the " Strength and safety of the nation lie in its, ability to produce what it requires from its own soil and factories." On the initiative of the Sheffield Chamber the word "Empire" was substituted for the word "Nation," and at -once the "Morning Post" stated that it had! no quarrel with this change of the wording of the resolution "so long as it is not taken to exclude the Protection of British agriculture." There at once we are up against one of -the greatest stumbling.-blocks In the .path of. Pro- tection. For again and 'again, it has been made abundantly clear .that the great territorial interests in ,our .Conservative ,party naturally, enough will never support or tolerate Protec- ,tive taxes for manufactured articles unless they receive very effective Protection at the same time for agricultural produce; and therefore Canadian wheat, or Australian mutton, which now finds a free market with us,, to our immense benefit, would have to encounter duties fairly substantial even at the outset, and which, as all experience has shown, have a dangerous tendency to grow to large proportions once they are imposed. Does that seem to be a policy calculated to strengthen Imperial sentiment in. the long run, either from the point of view'of the Colonies who send us their produce, or the consumers at home who would have to pay so much more dearly for it?

div.head: IF GERMANY ADOPTS FREE TRADE
div.p: IF GERMANY ADOPTS FREE TRADE

Again, among those who have suffered most terribly in this war is France; and are we then to signify our deep respect and admiration for the splendid valour and fortitude of our bril- liant Ally across the Channel by imposing onerous duties on hat`o she sends us? Is France likely to appreciate such a change of British .policy, or is she, on Oho contrary, at the present time making it sufficiently clear that this is exactly what she does not want ?

div.p: Theatre Managers And Foot- ballers Do Not Mind.
CHEERFUL VIEWS.

The most interesting impositions in the Bud- get, introduced last luesday, are the taxes on theatres, cinemas and football matches. They are not the least popular either. The tax amounts to Id. on a 2d. fee or under, and rises to is. on 12s. 6d. The-amusement hall managers in Wariington are not at all worried, all agreeing that this is a just tax. Mr. W. A. Jackson, manager of the Palace and Hippodrome, was• quite pleasant about it. "We don't mind it a bit," hc said. "Of course, the public will have to pay, arid I don't think they should mind, for entertainments are far cheaper than they really should be. Wheriyokk consider the 'high prices paid to some of the' artistes, you are bound to agree with me. I do ; not think it will affect the attendances at all." Would such a change of policy be any the more popular among the neutral nations, whether they were invited to pay the same duties as the Allied Powers, which they would certainly 'dislike; or whether, in order to give the Allies a preference, they had to pay still higher dUties, which they would as certainly and very strongly resent? Should we not by such a policy run the risk of playing straight into Germany's hands, and the more so if Germany, finding it impossible with a half-starved popu- lation to re-impose her high Protective tariff at the conclusion of the war, were to adopt a system of Free Trade, or something very pear it, and so tack on the advantages of cheap material of production to the scientific method in which she excels ?

div.head: WE SHOULD PAY THE TAX.
div.p: WE SHOULD PAY THE TAX.

Turning to our own special problems at home, it is urged in many quarters, and, for instance, even Lord Cromer tells us that we must impose a general tariff to help us to pay for the enor- mous cost of the war. But is there in political economy any single proposition more generally admitted than the palpable fact that, broadly speaking, import duties are paid by the nation which imposes them? •A good many people have a hazy idea that the imposition of these duties, for instance on German goods, will enable us indirectly to compel Germany to pay us something, at any ratei of an indemnity. But these duties would have a precisely con- trary effect. It is our own people who would find the money—in other words, who would pay the tax—which we expected to get out of Germany, and that is quite a different pro-1 position; and they will have to pay a good deal more money besides, inasmuch as they would have to reckon with largely increased pripes for all the food-stuffs and mann- fittured articles produced at home, the, prices of which would have been advanced to an extent equivalent to the Pro- -1 tective duties imposed. That policy might pos- sibly be to the advantage of a certain .section of territorial and commercial, magnates. But would it in the end be a policy likely to make for the general well-being and content of our people, and for our political-stability?' We are told that at the end of this war we must -be prepared, for political, •and even sentimental reasons, to sacrifice some of our most cherished principles and convictions, Possibly. I would not for a moment venture to assert the 'contrary. By all means let us bring an open mind and unbiassed judgment to bear upon the tremendous problems ahead of us; but, on the other hand, let us think twice and thrice before we rashly commit our- selves to crude and ill-considered experiments,, by which instead of gaining substantial advan- tages in either respect, we may lose heavily both from a sentimental and from a .political point ef view, and at the same time sustain even heavier and more serious cotamercial loss. When slap-dash politicians and reckless journalists would fain rush us nowadays into ill-considered experiments, is it not time to cry: "Hold; have a care lest in playing fast and loose with great principles of commercial polity, under which we have • achieved and ' maintained for ourselves a marvellous position in the commercial markets of the world, and under which the people of our country have enjoyed a wonderful measure of comparative prosperity, we play into the hands of those one-time commercial rivals who are to-day our bitterest enemies" ?-..Yours, A. After a trying illness, Mrs. Smethurst, wife of Alderman James Smethurst, 'died at her residence, 8, Bewsey-place,' -on -Sunday morn- ing, at the age of .eighty years. it is no exag- geration to say th,Wthe'whole of her long life was filled with good ,actions in both the domes- tic and social spheres. Naturally, the needs of the war called into activity, even in failing health, one who was •,so sympathetic towards the afflicted, and so energetic in behalf of those needing help. She set up a machine of her own for making bandages . and bought large quantities of material dud was made into socks and other articles which go under the general name of soldiers' comforts, 'which she sent to the various centres of distribution.
Aldernia,n Smethurst made an ideal Mayor

div.head: REV. W. BRACECAMP'S TRIBUTE AT FUNERAL.

Everybody who knew Mrs. Smethurst loved her. -None ,of her friends would ‘ever forget her year of _office as Mayoress. What a help she was 'to her husband! She worked hard for it, and up till the very last she was always inquiring about and Was par- ticularly anxious that God's work in this neighbourhood should prosper. Alderman and Mrs. Smethurst had been travelling to- gether along life's -pathways for many, many years, and had been real helpmeets to each other. Whether they sacrificed their lives on the battlefield for all that was noble and just, or whether they died- peacefully in their homes, might God give them peace and might they be ready !

div.head: Failure of the Apostle Paul.
div.p: The Failure of the Apostle Paul.

In concluding a series *of lectures on "The I Apostolic Age" last' Friday, Mr. A. Monnfield completed an interesting survey of the 'life and 1 labours of the Apostle Paul. The ordinary view that the work of the Apostle was successful and that he laid the foundation of the Early Church was declared by the lecturer to be incorrect. Paul's missionary efforts were overshadowed by a great difficulty which arose out of the caste spirit of the Jewish Christians. The Church at Jerusalem never grasped in any complete way the teachings of Jesus. It never realised the world-wide mission of Christianity and made no missionary efforts. Paul with finer vision grasped three important truths, that- Christianity was a religion of spirit and not of 'ritual, that it was, a universal religion and a religion of character. His vies were assailed by the Jerusalem Christians who followed him from city to city, teaching that Christianity wag a Jewish religion, and that the Gentiles could not become Christians unless they first became 'Jews. His work was largely undone by these Judaising teachers. After his death his in- fluence waned and ritualistio ideas fastened themselves upon the Church. It was not , until Luther that his great teachings were discovered and attained power. George Fox got the inner meaning of the Galatian letter and made it powerful in England. The ritualism of the Medieval Church was 'Jewish in its nature and not Christian. So also was the belief in predestination which held the Churches, Roman, Anglican and Puritan in its grip until the day of Wesley. The belief in election was essentially Jewish and not yet was the .Christian Church rid of it. With the ediscovery of Paul had come the Reformation, and the Quaker ard Methodist revivals, and greater things. yet wo,ll-' come as he was better understood.. Paul had not vet come to his own. His enlightened teaching that "there was neither Jew nor Greek nor male nor female in Christ Jesus" would- yet end war and solve our. social 'problems.

Bishop Of Liverpool On The
Welfare Of Girls.

"We‘have reason to thank God we are liVing at the .time of this war. God caused us to, be born in this country so that we might each one of us do something for the furtherance of our country," declared the Bishop of Liverpool (Dr. Chavasse) in an adaress he delivered to a crowded congregation of women at the Lenten service held at the Parish Church, Warrington, on Friday afternoon. He asked women to do what they could to com- fort and .help those in sorrow, and tell them of the infinite love of God. They should think of the young girls who were, perhaps, a little indiscreet. It was not vice or infamy, but in the great majority of eases, curiosity—a sort of infatuation for the man in khaki. The young women of to-day would be a great power in tha country when the war was over, and their wel- fare should be regarded as a sacred duty. _ _

It as certain that when the war was over we should have to face the most difficult and troublous times in our history. One way in which women could help was by practising thrift. It was a true saying that every pound they wasted they gave to the Germans, and every pound they saved they gave to their own .country. Women should inculcate thrift among. their chiltiren and practise frugality in the home.

div.head: Selfishness Abandoned.
div.p: Selfishness Abandoned.

The Lord Bishop, addressing a congregation of men in the evening, said increase of wealth had brought with it a growth of self-indulgence. and though there was much good-natured kind- ness to be found, yet the vast number of peopb seemed to be living for ,two objects—to have good time and to make ‘money. With the dec- laration of war all this :was changed, and there was a star of self-sacrifice revealed with all its splendour and beauty. Millions of parents gave up with pangs in their heart's, and tears in their eyes, their greatest earthly treasures. The soldiers on the battlefield displayed the forget- fulness of self, and showed a, devotion to duty, which fired their countrymen far and wide. When the danger of the war was really under- stood the people, high and low, gave out of their riches or poverty, larger sums of money than had ever, been contributed before. The signal of self-sacrifice Was love' for God. The country, and friends. Selfishness hid God, but Iself-sacrifice taught them to know Him. Self- sacrifice also brought joy. The selfish man or 'Woman must. always be miserable and fail to taste some of the highest joys Which this world knew.

Soldiers . having abused the privilege of 2-,ding: on the Corporation trelacans and.omni- buees, the Town touncil 'decided on Tuesday to .withdraw. this privilege. div.head: PAINCIPLE INVOLVED.
div.p: A PAINCIPLE INVOLVED.
Town Council Decide Against
Widowed Mother.
TEMPORARY EMPLOYES' ALLOWANCES.

A long discus4on, and at one point a breeze, between. Alderman Tinnion and , Councillor Wilson, were the: outstanding features of a notice of motion moved by Councillor Wilson at the Town Council meeting on Tuesday.

The motion in effect asked the Council to make a grant of 58. per week to the mother of Tram- guard Ridyard, who had joined the Forces. A good deal of stress was laid on the fact thfft it waS a case of personal hardship, and it was pleaded that the Army allowance was not sufficient to keep her in bare comfort. Several Councillors agreed on these lines, but the general opinion was that Mrs. Ridyard had not suffered any hardship at all, and one member considered that she was now better oil finan- cially ;while her son was serving in the Army. It was pointed put that Ridyard was only tem- porarily emploS,ed by the Corporation, having previously been a barber's assistant, taking .up the post .of tram-guard in place of another employe, who had joined the Forces in the early-part Of the war. Eventually the motion was put to the Meeting, and the Mayor declared it defeated by a large Meieritv.

Councillor WILSON, in support of his motion, thought Ridyard's ease was a hard one, and by granting ss—to Ridyard's mother they, would enable her to keep her home over her head and have a little comfort. On all occasions, he said. they should be generous with their, soldiers. Ile could 'not understand anyone saying that a mother or any other dependent would be better off when the breadwinner was away at the war, taking his chance, and the possibility of losing a limb. He pleaded that it was a special case which ought to receive the consideration of the council. Ridyard's mother at the outside 'ivould receive 15s. in allowances, and the additional five shillings would bring the allowance up by El, and that was not too much: "Why, bless my soul," declared Mr. Wilson, " I have heard one member say it costs him 10s. per week for cigars." • - Councillor CTJNNINGTON seconded -

div.head: PRINCIPLE INVOLVED.
div.p: THE PRINCIPLE INVOLVED.

The DEPUTY MAYOa said tram-guard Ridyard took the place ot another man, who had joined the Forces and v/ho received an allowance from the Corporation. Itwas not merely a matter of ss. a week, but of destroying a principle. • It was for the General Purposes Committee or that Council to say whether there should be any de- parture from the principle they had themselves laid down. Previous to entering the service of the Corporation, Ridyard was a :barber's assist. ant, and the most liberal estimate of his wages then was 15s. per week. If he had not became a conductor his mother could not have beeji much better off than she was now.. The acceptance•of Councillor Wilson's motion would be a breach of time 'principle • adopted by the Council.
Councillor WILSON said the man did•not leave his old place. • There was no work for him. When he entered the Corporation employ he allowed his mother 235. per week.

div.p: COMPASSION %;. LOGIC.

Councillor lIENSIIALL agreed that the Council would be going back upon their previous resolu- tion if they decided to make a grant: Ridyard had, however, been in the Corporation employ 11 months, and, while he took the position at his own risk, the committee were possibly to blame for taking a mkt of military age, in place of one who had gone. It might be that his Mother was no, worse off 'than, before,' but not merely on the ground of justice, but on the ground of mercy, he appealed to the Council to make a grant. " I Would ,rather bea member of a Council which violated not one resolution bnt 100 if by doing so at this time we could bring a little bit of comfort or euse to those to whom money compensation is infinitesimal" add.d Councillor llenshall. •

Councillor ROBERTS argued in support of the motion, and said although the scale of allow:. ances applied to those persons who were in the employ of the Corporation; on August 10th, 1914, it did not necessarily 'restrict the Council if they thought It to make a compassionate allowance in any case. He did not think it excessive generosity to allow ss. a week to a widow. But he would rather a thousand times err in that direction than endeavour logically to justify an attitude which, while it wal in accordance with a previous resolution of the Council, might in individual cases prove hard.

div.p: NOT 4 CHARITABLE INSTITUTION.

Councillor DALE described :Councillor Wilson's action in bringing the matter before the Coun- cil as ill-advised. div.p: RESOLUTION SHOULD BE RESCINDED.

div.p: WELCOME AND RE-WELCOME.
Belgian Consul Among His People At Warrington.

Backed by the British and Belgian flags—the extremities of , each folding into those of the other, and so symbolising unity—and surrounded with beautiful flowers, plants, and tree ei in taste- ful arrangement and profusion, thb Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) and Councilfor Henry Roberts, chairman of the Refugees' Committee, in the Council Chamber, on Saturday afternoon, welcomed the Belgian Consul of Liverpool (M. Verspreeuwen) and re-welcomed about, a hun- dred Belgians, who came to Warrington fox succour soon after the commencement of hostili-

The scene was picturesque and the proceedings struck with subdued emotion. Sitting with .his elderly father 'was a Belgian soldier, who' had just arrived on leave from the trenches. The Ladies' Committee, who hdve been arduous in their service.and generous in their philanthropy, were present in full force and, in the Mayor's Parlour, each was thanked by the veteran Consul for her kindness.
• The Mayor spoke of the pleasure and pridc it had given the people of Warrington to make ;he Belgians comfortable, remarking that all in lieir power had been and would continue to be lone. _

_ Divining the purport of his remarks, the refugees applauded gratefully. Having thanked Warrington in particular, the Belgian Consul, speaking English fluently and charmingly, dwelt on the kindness of England generally. When the Belgians went back te their own country, he said, they would never forget what we had • done for them. Neither would the generations to come. The receptior given would be inscribed in golden letters in the annals of history. (Applause.) Admiration For England.

I like the English people," he continued. "I have lived amongst them for 42 years, and my admiration for them has always increased. As to what England has done in, this war there i. no justification either for grumbling or criticising. She has done more than anyone could have dreamt of her doing. What had she got in 1914? A great Navy, but a comparatively small Army and no munitions. To-day you have got at least 3,000,000 soldiers, plenty of munition .- for yourselves, and you have given munitions also to France, Belgium and Russia. And then some say 'England has done nothing.' You have got every reason to do so and be proud of it. (Applause.) No Leniency For Germany.

"How longis this war going to last? It may last a little longer, but not much. When I was 'a boy I had a wise and learned uncle, who used to say 'lf England is concerned in anything she will come out top.' England is with, us now, and this war must finish in our favour. (Ap- plause.) "When the war is over we must not be too lenient with the German Empire—with those at the head of this German militarism, .who have tqo. much to say in everything."' (Applause.) In conclusion, the Consul observed that the Allies were fighting for all tillat was best in civilisation, "not just for ourselves, but for the whole world, and once eve had got the •German down he would 'never come up again." Councillor Roberts assured the Consul that the people of Warrington felt just as cordially ,to the Belgian people as the Belgians did to us. We had made friends with those who had come to us in their, distress and they had .gained our respect and admiration. The Belgians were a •brave nation, and, had'a King who was a model , Of what a King ought to be. (Applause.) The King might have 'lost his territory. 'but he barl not lost his son]. If the Getman Emperor had so far not lest his territory he had 'certainly already lost his soul and everything that made life worth living, because of his demonaical pas- sion to govern a small nation, whose very boots lie was not tit to black. The heart of every. Englishman had been stirred by the heroic de- fence which the Belgians had made against the enemy, and they could rest assured ,that we' should not hesitate to give every ounce of , strength and every ,pound we possessed' to gain victory. div.head: :COL CROSFIELD, D.S.O.
div.p: :COL CROSFIELD, D.S.O.
Wounded In The Ankle While Reconnoitring.
LEG AMPUTATED.
Colonel George Crosfield, D. 8.0., who was

only recently promoted from the rink of Major, was reported, early,in the week, to have been severely wounded. Yesterday we received the grave news that Colonel Crosfield had his left leg amputated below the knee on Tuesday, and that he had written to Sir Arthur Crosfield saying that he was receiving every attention and that the operation was inevitable, as the bone was much shattered.

div.head: BLOW FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: A BLOW FOR WARRINGTON.

'There is not a home in Warrington where sad news will not be received in sorrow. The early news—which did not seem so serious —was heard with alarm, showing how close the 'gallant Colonel was to the hearts of us all.
Wounded.

Ever since he went to the Front his doings have been followed locally with confidence and Admiration. He was out on March 31st engaged ,upon his favourite occupation of reconnoitring some ground, along with the Brigade Major, when he received a gun-shot wound on the right side of the left ankle, causing a com- pound fracture of the shin bone and the ac- 7tompanying fibula.. People sought comfort in the fact that the, evidence to hand did not Point to very serious developments. . The War Office, reported the injuries as "severe" only. Sir Arthur and 'Lady Crosfield, who wished to o to the Colonel's assistance immediately in the French hospital, were informed that the War Office issued passes in "dangerous" cases only. Again, the Colonel himself, writing to his sister, Mrs. Ryan, described the mishap as a "nuisance," though he added: don't suppose I shall be fit for the field under three months."

Last evening's news has revealed how serious the. matter 'really is, and symnathy will flow in from all hands for one who has so nobly played his part and who seemed destined to play a bigger part in the eomitiv tussle between Germany and the Allies.

div.head: LORD DERBY PIERROTS.
div.p: LORD DERBY PIERROTS.
Another Interesting Concert At
Winwick.

This account, as the Press Bureau would say, continues and supplements that of a fortnight ago in describing the night operations of the "Lord 'Derby Pierrots" at Winwick. ,They were all aboard again the other night, and the stage in the concert hall was a blaze of light, mirth, song and dance. They have not yet got to telling funny stories, although, being soldiers, they must know a few.- What? .For their efforts they, were this time rewarded with fifty cigarettes each, the "ladies," with becoming immodesty, also accepting them and tucking them away in their beautiful bouquets. The scene was like that of a first-night on the professional stage with "stars" in the cast, or a last-night among the .amateur theatricals. .As before, the entertainment evolved start- ling novelties. This khaki-Cum-black-and- white troupe have fertile minds and they converted the song "The Crocodile Crawl" into a musical sketch,' with something aston- ishingly grotesque at the tail-end, or, rather, the head of it. Following the singing of'• the sang by Private Pollington the party lined up each behind the other and their bent heads forming the animal's vertebr crawled along as lumberingly and realistically as if they had just swallowed an alligator. In the hands of the first was held horizontally the huge head of a crocodile, occasionally turned ferociously at the audience, but the men, used to bullets and shrapnel, did not flinch. . . . It was made of paper. An Aeroplane Raid..

But, perhaps, the greatest surprise of the et:ening was while Lance-Corporal Kerrigan was rendering "Paddy Malony's Irish Aero- plane," bombs dropping with sickening thuds (buckets .in the wings, one suspected), howls from the chorus, and the rapid progress across the fly of the stage of a toy aeroplane—a Pemberton Billing model, more or less. Another particularly good item was that of "China Town," all the pierrots% twirling Orientally decorated paper sunshades and the leading singer, Rifleman Gordon (lath of the Carl Rosa Opera Company) playing affection- ately, like a "Sweet Seventeen," with his pig-tail. It was a charming episode. Private Hughes Scored a success with his rendering of "Somewhere a Voice is Calling." In this case it was a whistle. r. . . He is an expert in this medium of musical expression. Private Pollington and "Lady" Huggins con- tributed a clever exhibition of the .Tango, Mexican and Argentine. style.

div.head: BOY KILLED.
div.p: BOY KILLED.
The Danger Of Alighting From
A Tramcar.

Fltiling to ,hear the warning shout of the Ira driver, Harry Hannan, the seven-year- old son of Mr. John Edward Hannan, baker and confectioner, 36, Parker-street, .stepped froth behind a tramcar from which he . had just alighted, and was knocked down and killed by a taxicab, driven by John Wilfred Paterr son, 741, Knutsford-road, of the firm of Pater- son and Son.
Tito inquest was conducted at the Warrington Police Station on Monday morning by Deputy- Coroner F. A. Jones.

John Wilfred, Paterson, the taxicab driver,' said that at 6.5 on Thursday, the 29th of March, he was driving his taxicab along 'Knnts ford-mad, in the direction of Warrington. The - tramcar was . stopped near the end of St. Mary-street, and ' he continu- ously ,sounded his horn to warn people getting off the car of his approach. Just as he was passing the boy rushed out in front of his car, and elthough be swerved to the left, the front of the car struck him. Witness pulled up, picked, up the boy, and removed him to the Infirmary, but he was dead on arrival. The taxi was travelling at ten miles an hour. The Coroner: How far did you go after strik- ing the boy F—About the length of the car. .Did you notice whether the boy 'looked in your direction?—No, sir. Joseph Wilkinson, 20, Griffiths-street, the driver of the tramcar, said that he received- a signal to stop at St. Mary-street. He did so, and on looking inside the tramcar he noticed the boy getting off. He noticed the ' taxicab approaching, and it occurred to him that the boy might run across the road. Accordingly, he 'shouted to him to stop .where he was, but, :evidently not .hearing the warning, the boy darted across the road. He stepped from his car, and found the hey lying in the roadway, the driver having pulled up a few yards away. The bcty got up, and after walking a few yards collaprd. . QuAioned by the. coroner as to whether the line at that spot was a single or' double one, witnegs replied that it was a double line. There would be a distance of about ten feet between the car and the footpath.

div.head: PASSING TRAMCARS.
div.p: PASSING TRAMCARS.

The Coroner said he asked the question be- cause, although it was not so in this case, it was within the knowledge of all of them that some taxi-cars did go too quickly in, passing tramcars that were setting down or taking up passengers, and that the roadway was narror between the cars and the footpath.
Witness said the lady conductor was on the top collecting fares. Mr. Hannan: Is School-street a stopping station?—Yes.
Can you .tell me why he was not put down at School-streetP—No; I cannot be reiponsible for both ends of the car.

Mr. Hannan: He should have been put dawn there; that is all I have to say. • Frederick Benson, a general labourer, 224, Knutsford-road, said that he noticed the taxi- cab approaching at a speed which he estimated at ten miles an hour. The boy ran from behind the car, in front of the motor, and both the off-wheels passed over him. The driver did everything pcissible, even running his car into a brick *all in order to avoid the acci- dent.

Detective Sumner said he had made very careful inquiries, and there Was other evidence to the same effect. It would appear thaf the boy seemed very excited when he found he had gone beyond his proper stopping-place and danced about the car.

div.head: STAGE AND KINEMA.
div.p: STAGE AND KINEMA.
Royal Cowl.

, Although the visit of Mr. Ernest E. Norris- and Company in a round of brilliant London successes has been appreciated, I wish there had been' crowded houses each night, for the plays and players are' far above the average. "The Lion and the Mouse," "John Glayde's Honour," and "The Walls of Jericho," have' each earned distinction and long life.

As the Magnate—magnet--Mr. Norris is superb: His powerful personality is excellently suited to parts of this character. "All gigantic financiers and . thinkers in material goods smoke one cigar after another," remarka The Mouse. When I entered Mr.. Norris's dressing-room and offered him a cigarette he declined with thanks. "No," he said,. "I don't mind you, but I .don't want your cigar- ettes. 'ln 'The Lion and the. _fousb' I have to "get through five ".cigars, and that is quite enough smoking. • You •know what stage cigars .are—just 'consumable !" he added subtly.

Mr. _Norris holds a record. He has played more leading parts in West •End plays ,than anyone. Northern audiences are his latest love. "My stuff is above the average," he confessed, modestly. "At one time only the South appre- ciated it, but I now find that towns in the North, particularly. Lancashire and Yorkshire, get enthusiastic. There has been an improve- ment in their taste in recent years."

John Glayde in "John Glaydsi's ,Honour" is Mr. Norris's best yet. most exhaasting char- acter. Being the "Iron Bing," with millions of pounds at stake, and torn by' lealousy in his domestic life, takes it out of one, as the phrase goes. "I never play it above one night a week," he told me. ; "The -strain is too much. Anyone in the company will tell you it is my nervn,night. I " must never lose sight of the character, and all my attention has to be concentrated on it."

Mr. Norris was here twelve months ago. Be- fore then twenty years divided his previous visit. He ca.me with Clarence Holt. He is not only an interpreter, but a creator, having had two or three successful plays, and being now 'engaged on, the writing of another, with, a business super-man as the central character. Mr. Norris tells me that he procured Seymour Hicks his 'first speaking part, and that the great Chevalier was once under his manage- ment at two guineas a week.

The 'leading lady, Miss Ray Parry, has shown rare'ability and charm. She is delight- ful and. has always been associated in the pro- duction of first-class plays. She started with Mr. F. R. Benson—and you, know what that. means.' You have to be a person of quality. Miss Parry has also served with the Liverpool Repertory Company and has *played the lead in Mr. Harold-Neilson's "Diana of Dobson's.P She was acting with the great Van Biene at Brighton when he died on the stage.

We are to have a revue next week. -" Heave-o !" Sounds nautiCal, and it is. There is only. One scene—the deck of a ship. Money is being spent on holding good artistes and not an excess of scenery. Tito 'artistes include Charles Harvey, as "Bill Stickers." A very funny man, he. Rene Ash is the leading lady, and, besides being of beautiful appearance, she has a delightful way with her; also a very accept- able voice.
A "full London chorus of bathing beauties, flighty' flappers, and promiscuous promenaders" are promised. Oh, let us be joyful!
Hippodrome.

Just a dozen words about this week's revue, "Step This Way." It has justified expecta- tions. Billy. Leonard,. the Dude, has been a graft success. He is an Irish boy of culture, who believes that the day of, the red-nosed comedian is past. He. has been one hiniself.
Next week there is to be another strong programme, headsxl by David Devant, the

famous magician. Charming in manner and good-humoured, he is original and mystifying, and has attended two Royal, Command per- formances. That speaks volume. On the occasion of the visit of the King and Queen to Warrington, Mr. Devant appeared before them at Knowsley Hall in the evening, and that "bluff Lancashire man" (Lord Derby) in- formed him that Their liajesties desired him tb give "some more."" That speaks more volumes.

. It is interesting to note that Devant followed the royal motor cars through Warrington to Knowsley and recehted cheers from the crowd. as did members of the royal suite itself. At first, being taken for what he was not, was rather embarrassing, but the crowd cheered and cheered, and then he thought he might as well bow his acknowledgments. . . . He is a. great illusionist.

Devant has been before the public for thirty years. Everyone has heard of him. He is as well known as the great Horatio.. He has some wonderful illusions, and is respected by his brother Illusionists to such an extent that they have presented him with an appreciative address. Big audiences are expected next week,

As a rule, we arrange inter-platoon football competitions, which are always a 'great success, and concerts. behind the lines are a common oCcurrence."

Asked when he thought the war would be over, he replied: ".Very soon; for we have plenty of men, plenty of guns, and, what is more, plenty of ammunition, for every shell the Germans fire at us we giye Ahem at least six hack." _

The excellent work done by the Y.M.C.A. Centres, both, at home and abroad, has been subject to *more than passing prairie. Its 'keen appreciation by the men is only equalled by that of their. officers and the Y.M.C.A. huts have come to play an almost indispensable part in the daily life of the King's Armies. The Y.M.C.A : huts are . now open to every man wearing the King's uniform—whatever his creed or faith, he is made welcome. Sev- eral thousands sleep under their roofs in London every night on their way to and from the trenches and their homes. At 'the commencement oft war there was not a single-centre in France and the first .40 cases of books were sent out at Christmas, 1914.: To-day there are -127-centres in France alone, and have been established at Salonica, _Egypt; Malta, and, in fact, everywhere where. our ,troops are .to be- found. Who does not :welcome a letter- bearing the, well-known triangle upon its cover? That letter..might never have been written but for.; the Y.M.C.A. hut, where Pen, paper, warmth, light and .comfort are provided, and the men's thoughts' -turned towards home. A short time ago Mrs. Alec Tweedie, of London, • issued a national appeal for huts, stating that one could be built and equipped at' the cost ! of £3OO, and a few people in Lymm took this appeal up, with the idea in mind of raising the necessary sum, and having a hut erected and christened "The Lymm and, - District Tint." By brihging this scheme to a success the people of Lymm have helped materially in checkmating the little Prussian scheme of humiliating Britain. The necessary sum has been raised by an energetic band of workers, who organised sales, concerts, house-to-house collections, &c., and their efforts have borne tangible results.

•Mr. Walter Ashton, who is an unattested single man, and adjutant of the Warrington Volunteer Defence Corps, appeared before the Recruiting Tribunal on Monday afternoon, and stated his reasons for "his attitude in staying out of the Forces." Applicant said he was a partner in the firm of Messrs. W. and A. Ashton, builders, and was indispensable to the business. He had heavy financial obligations owing to being senior in the firm, which was started 15 years ago by a loan from one of his brothers. By hard work and capitalised savings, now sunk in plant, and the carrying out of contract work their 'turnover had greatly increased. Twenty five of their staff .had joined the Colours, three of whom—married, men—having done so on consideration that the. firm took them back after the war. Among the contracts 'they had been engaged on was the building Of a munitions works, and they had also executed work for the Lord Derby War Hos- pital. Their financial obligations were such that if they were unable to meet them there would be hardship not only to themselves, but to others, if the business had to be wound up. Witness added that he .was also a managing director of the Palatine Rinks and the Grand Electric Theatre. "I have no desire to shirk my duty to the State," declared the applicant. My brotnei and myself served the country during the South African War, and now all my spare time is being devoted to training myself and others in the Volunteers in case of invasion." He added that the house he was bred and born in would be closed down if he were sent to the Colours. The Chairman of the Tribunal (Alderman Tinnion): You are a member of the Volunteer Training Corps—Yes. I am acting as adjutant. Didn't you promise you would enlist if called apon?—Before I joined the Corps I submitted my case to Colonel Mocatta, who was the mili- tary representative, and he said mine Was a '-proper case for the Corps. The Chairman: But you declined to attest. I remember that you went to the Baths and were medically examined, but would not take the oath of allegiance: You had some grievance with the conditions of enlisting. You said we were enlist- ing men under false pretences, • and that every- thing was a fwd. Applicant ciPlnurred from this, but the Chair- man said he remembered the incident quite well. _ _ . _
_ Captain Mathams recollected that Mr. Ashton "expressed some reasons why ho should not attest." _ .

Applicant said that he certainly turned up at the Drill Hall later in order to attest, but Captain Mathams was not there. Captain MAthams: Is your brother appealing? —He is attested. I don't know whether he is going to appeal. I suggest that if he does his case should be taken on its merits at the time. Applicant was exempted until the 30th June.

At the same sitting there were also several conAcientious objectors. • Asked to give his reason. for being a conscien- tious objector, Ernest L. Ince, of Forrest-street, said as a Socialist he was opposed to war, and he could not take part in it because he really did not think it would be of any benefit to the class to which he belonged. Applicant, in reply to the Chairman, said he was willing to serve his country in a civil capacity, but not military. The Chairman: Are you prepared to do some- thing which will prevent the foul deeds which have been committed in England over the week- end ?—l' am' prepared to do anything in a. civil capacity. Do you object to go into non-combatant ser- vice?—l would rather not.

The Chairman: The appeal is refused, and you will go where the military send you. As he left the room, Ince said he would appeal to the County Tribunal. Walter N. lace, brother to Ernest Ince, appealed on the ground that he was in a reserved occupation, but it was pointed out to appellant that only employers appealed on trade grounds. Appellant then intimated that, like his brother, he was a conscientious objector, but he did not put this in his appeal, in the first in- stance, because he was assured that he was in a reserved trade.

The Chairman pointed out that the firm hati withdrawn their appeal on the man's behalf. Applicant, in reply to tile military repre- sentative, denied that he had developed a conscientious objebtion since his appeal was put in. The appeal was refused; appellant' also stating that he would appeal to the County Tribunal.

div.head: CONSCIENCE AND EAST •COAST RAIDS.
div.p: CONSCIENCE AND EAST •COAST RAIDS.
The third conscientious objector was John H. Elwell (19), of Lovely-lane. With an air of confidence he told the Tribunal "that war is wrong, and God did not make man to take his fellow Man's life."

The Chairman: You don't think it wrong to defend yourself ?—Yes. Supposing a young man tackled you, would you defend yourself should try and prevent it. 'But I would not fight him. Fighting would be against my conscience. Doesn't your conscience tell you to do some. thing to prevent such terrible scenes as we have heard of on the East Coast and the murder of innocent children F—No.

You will do nothing. Have you a mother or any sisters? Will you see them killed ?—lf 1 could prevent it I would d 9 so. How would you do it—by force F—Not by force. I would take them away. Asked if he would do something to relieve the sufferings of wounded soldiers, appellant said if he went to their aid he would be only helping to get them better, to be sent to the Front again.
Refused. CONSCIENCE AND A MAN WITH A GUN.

The other. appellant with a " conseienos " WriS Charles Casey, of 239, Winwick-road. As a Socialist he thought war was wrong, and he was questioned as to his reason for believing this. Appellant replied that he did not think it right that he should butcher his fellow man.
The Chairman: Do you object to being butchered yourself P—Yes. Asked how he would stop the war, appellant said we should agitate for peace and stop fight- ing.

The Chairman replied that they never argued with a man with a. gun. Appellant was in agreement .with strikes, as they prevented men being cowed down. The Chairman said that was a good illustra- tionnf the present position. If we did not fight we would be cowed down. Refused.

That a Compulsory Service Bill for all mar- ried men be passed, under which the calling up shall coincide with the respective groups under the Derby Scheme; • That we protest against any moratorium and demand legislation with a view to providing means to keep men's homes inviolate during their absence.

The above constituted the demands of the Warrington Branch of the National Union of Attested Married Men, as passed at a meeting held in the Co-operative Hall on Sunday. They were embodied in a resolution which was unanimously passed and ordered to be fel'. warded to the Prime Minister, Lord Derby, and Mr. Harold Smith (the local member in Parliament). There would be an atteridance of about 200, presided over by Mr. Herbert Johnson, who was supported on the platforui by Mr. P. G. Wright, Mr. A. Clay, Mr. Graham (treasurer), Mr. S. Bradburn (secretary), Mr. Mac Duff, Mr. H. Meadowcroft (Blackburn) and Mr. C. F. Rymer (Liscard).

div.head: NOT TO AVOID SERVICE.
div.p: NOT TO AVOID SERVICE.

The Chairman, addressing the gathering as "Comrades of the Battalion," said that if any man joined the movement with the idea that by some device he would be able to avoid ser- vice he would be' very much mistaken. As far as that branch was concerned, such was not their purpose. In the great crisis of the coun- try it was their duty to show their sympathy, gratitude and loyalty by every means in their power, either by civil' or military service, so as to bring the war to a successful issue. Any- thing else would be unthinkable. He did not appeal to the married men of Warrington to join the union with the object of avoiding service; ; they wanted to safeguard their businesses and homes as far as possible. (Hear. hear.) He believed Lord Kitchener wanted the men, and the Government were endeavour- ing to provide them. If the, Government were responsible for the recruiting muddle, then the quicker a solution was found for it the better; even if they had all to get into khaki. Conscription All Round.

"Now we have started conscription let us go the whole hog," exclaimed the Chairman. He did not agree with the cry "Single men first." He would rather see compulsion applied to all classes of men of physical fitness under the age of 45. Conscription did not sound nice in this country, but we had it now in a most unjust and inequitable form. (Hear, hear.) The man who had built up a business and was living in a house which the present Army allowance' would not pay the rent was in a serious position if he had to go. Was it fair that an unattested competitor should be allowed to say "I have not been had" and remain behind and collar the business of the soldier? ("No.l If they could not have equality of sacrifice they could try and get something near,it.

div.head: RIGHT AND JUSTICE.
div.p: RIGHT AND JUSTICE.

Mr. H. Mea,dowcroft (one of the deputation who waited upon Lord Derby last Monday), in proposing the resolution, said that all the married men. required was a straight deal. He considered that the treatment of the attested married men was one of the most glaring pieces of trickery which had over disgraced the Government's administration of the war. They were not squealing, but they demanded that the pledges of the Government should be kept in an honest English-like manner. It was in the national interests that the-married men should not go, until the _single Men had .gone. He did not mean all single men, but the single men who were promised by the Gov- ernment, not including those who had been in munition works all their lives. He thought they had a right to request that the notice calling the first eight married groups should be cancelled until the single men had. gone. The union were not for selfishness, but merely for right and justice. The passing of the Military Service Act only gave the conscript an advantage- over the attested married man. On the day it was passed the Government starred and bodged 100,000 men in reserved occupations. They, -as Married men, asked that the list should be revised. It was mar: vellous how many city single men, followers of Charlie Chaplin, were. now engaged in such scientific work as milking cows. -(Laughter„) It would be interesting to know .how many single men had gone into new occupations before the Bill was passed. There were thou- sands of men in munition factories who ought to be in khaki at the present time„ As mar- ried men they conscientiously objected to fight for the so-called conscientious objector. The Only. Father • and the Only Husband. He had the greatest respect for the widowed 'mother's only son, but had not a wife an only husband and children an only father? Could anyone explain the difference in their positions? Even at this time he believed single men were being starred in the slipper industry. It would be a terrible thing if they had no slippers in war-time. (Laughter.) A married man would not require them in the trenches. The attitude of the Government had been disgraceful and most unsatisfactory; and the pledges of the Prime Minister were in keeping with his policy of "wait and see?" On December Bth Mr. Asquith said the, homes of marls:xi 'sien ivould be considered. Surely it did not iake sis.teen weeks•to consider that question. Married men did not intend to have a moratorium. They did not want to come back, after fighting the country's battles, to find a debt hanging round their necks which they would never get rid of. The married man waS beginning to realise that God helped those who helped themselves. Shuffles and More Promises.

. In outlining the Government's proposals for Married men, Mr. Walter Long commenced by defending Lord Derby, but the latter would riot :require Mr. Long to defend him if he had kept his pledges. Mr. Long stated that Lord Derby never promised to give the attested married men an advantage over the unottested. If (continued the speaker) Lord Derby never made such a promise there was someone else ,in the Government who did. All that they asked was that the unattested should not he given an advantage over -them. ( Applause.) The speeches of Mr. , Long would not bluff 'them. The -whole policy of the Government was a series of shuffles and prom:ses, and Mr. Long's speech consisted of shuffles and more promises. Married Men did not want charity. If the Government wanted them, to make sacrifices they ought to see that their wives and children were kept comfortable whilst they were away. Every man of military age, if physically fit, ought to take his share in the burden, and the burden equally distributed. Dining the recruiting scheme all over the country posters were exhibited bearing the notice: "No Attestation; No Appeal.' The unattested married Man did not want an appeal; he wanted* the job of the attested. (Hear, hear.) It was under •a threat of com- pulsion that the married men attested. He considered it was the duty of the Government to bring in a Bill for compulsion for all men of military age, and, to do it quickly. mi.. Asquith had stated that he would not be a party to any scheme of compulsion for married men. That stiatement would not be accepted .a.S satifo'actory or final. If the Prime Minister Would not agree to compulsion, let him make way for someone else. (Applause.) A Boom In Weddings.

The married men were given to understand before they attested - that all men who were single on August 15th would be deemed as such; but when the Compulsion Bill was brought forward (after they had been had) it was stated by the Government that all men single on November 2nd shall he presumed as single men. During that three months something like 100,000 got married and were now outside the 800 Pe of the Military service Act. The promises had not been kent and the Government had been guilty of dallying and delaying. in an obligation of' honour. Lord Derby had made an apPeal to the Patriotism of. the attested married man. div.head: RELIEF OF BELGIUM.
div.p: RELIEF OF BELGIUM.
Saving A Stricken Nation From
Starvation.

A striking indictment of Germany's continued inhumanity to Belgium and a powerful plea on behalf of the millions who, although destitute, remain loyal in that outraged country, are con- tained in the following important statement. It is signed by the Lord Mayor of London, as chairman of the National Committee for Relief in Belgium, by the Archbishop of Canterbury, Cardinal Bourne, the Moderator of the Church of Scotland, the President of the Free Church Council, the Chief Rabbi, the Duke of Norfolk, Lords Lansdowne, Rosebery, and Bryce, Mr. Arthur Henderson, Mr. John Redmond, Mr. Shirley Benn (hon. treasurer), and Mr. W. A. M. Goode (hon secretary).
To. the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—Eleven months ago w formed the National Committee for Relief in Belgium, and appealed to our fellow-subjects throughbut the British Empire on behalf of a million and a half Belgians; oppressed and threatened with starvation in their own outraged country. The number of destitute Belgians .inßelgium to-day exceeds three millions. Most of these are "women and children.

Since we made our previous appeal it has been conclusively proved that the Germans, contrary to every civilised precedent, will adhere to their "openly expressed intention not to support the Belgian population or supply them with food!! The words quoted are those used by Lord Robert Cecil, on behalf of the Government, in the House of Commons on January 27th last. That Lord Robert Cecil does not over-estimate the calculated cruelty of the German intention is shown by the fact that in Poland, where there is no neutral channel for the distribution of relief, the civilian population have been allowed to die like flies, and over 300,000 able-bodied Polish men have been driven into Germany, there to work in the mines and industries, thus freeing 300.000 Germans to go to the fighting front. The same thing would undoubtedly happen in Belgium but for food which reaches the Belgians through the Allies.

div.head: Germans Don't Benefit.
div.p: Germans Don't Benefit.

It has also been definitely ascertained that the food sent into Belgium does not reach or benefit the Germans. Lord 'Robert Cecil, on February 21st last, stated in the House of Commons that the "Government are satisfied with the manner in which the Relief Commission has carried on its work, :and have exacted guarantees from the German authorities who might otherwise have taken advantage of the. supplies." The confidential evidence of Belgians of repute, allowed out of Belgium, and of reliable neutrals, permitted into Belgium, confirms this offieial declaration. The neutral Relief Commission, of which Mr. Herbert Hoover is chairman, and which is conducted under the supervision of the American and Spanish diplomatic representa- tives, has been accurately described by Earl Curzon as "an absolute miracle of scientific organisation, synonymous with economy and efficiency combined." Receipts from the 2,700 Belgian Communes show that every ton of food imported into Belgium has been faithfully dis- tribtited by Belgians to Belgians under the close supervision of this Commission and its self- sacrificing American workers. The British National Committee, with the approval of the British and Belgian Governments, hands all its funds, without any deduction, to Mr. Hoover's Commission to be expended in food. In the conviction that thw methods of distri- buting relief in Belgium render it practically impossible for any appreciable quantity of the food to get into German hands, and with the evidenco, to justify this conviction, we do not hesitate again urgently to appeal to the British nation for further contributions. Our original appeal. up .to date, has brought in over £3,500,000, but this is almost £1,000,000 short of what is reouired, from British benevolent sources, to enable the destitute in Belgium to maintain life with loyalty. Of the total so far received, more than .£1,000.000 hits come from Australia and New Zealand. Our Debt of Honour.

Ovler seven million defenceless civilian's in Belgium, for more than a year. and a half, have suffered a tyranny almost inconceivable to those in our own uninvaded land. Nevertheless, they have maintained a resistance none the less courageous because it must be passive,. and, with almost negligible exceptions, they have re- fused to work for the Germans. Practically half of the whole of this population in Belgium, through no fault of their own, are now deltitute and live on a pitiful ration.

Is there any debt of honour more pressing or any work of .humanity with a stronger claim than that of helping to keep body and soul to- gether in the men, women, and children , in Belgium, who, in spite of misery and privation, endure all things and loyally await the coming of the Allies?

Donations and regular subscriptions, for which we most earnestly ask, should be. sent to Dominion, Colonial, or Local Committees, wherever they have been formed, or to Mr. • A.
